item.title: What kind of beast is an "internal OpenAI model " and why is DeepSeek catching up to OpenAI?
item.description:
Internal models of frontier labs are not publicly available. I don't really believe in conspiracy theories like "OpenAI has a real AGI in its basement and is only releasing a cut-down ChatGPT." The model used by its own researchers and the model sold through the API don't have to be the same. Frontier labs create not one neural network, but a factory of models: research checkpoints > experimental models > reward models > teacher models > models for generating synthetic data > model evaluators > distilled students > production models, and only the last element of the chain reaches the public. Why distillation is needed Suppose you've trained a monstrously expensive model that reasons well, writes code, and solves math problems, but each query to it costs enormous computational resources. For an in-house researcher, it's a working tool, and it's worth it if trillion-dollar markets are at stake. For a product with 100 million users, scaling access to such models is profitable, so instead of running it for every query, it's made into a teacher: it generates high-quality answers, solutions, reasoning trajectories, synthetic data, sometimes probability distributions themselves, and a smaller student is trained on this behavior, which doesn't need to reproduce the teacher entirely, but only transfer the necessary capabilities. This is one form of knowledge distillation, and the practice is so common that OpenAI directly provides developers with an official Model Distillation workflow: take answers from a stronger model, like GPT-4o or o1-preview, and train a cheaper model on them. OpenAI's own wording is quite precise: take an advanced model and achieve comparable quality on a specific task at a significantly lower cost. From this follows a rather simple thing: the best research model and the best production model are optimized for different functions, because the research model maximizes capabilities, while the production model has to simultaneously balance intelligence, latency, GPU cost, throughput, reliability, and safety. Read more

item.title: Simulating 30 Million Microbes in the Browser
item.description:
WebGPU provides direct access to modern graphics card capabilities, not just for rendering but also for general-purpose computing via compute shaders. But how far can this be pushed in a regular browser? What happens when computations involve a full-fledged simulation with tens of millions of objects? We'll explore this in the article. Read more

item.title: Architecture is more important than the model: how document processing is changing in the era of AI
item.description:
— In this project, we need to recognize documents well. — And what does "well" mean? — AI is everywhere now. I upload a document to a chat, and it answers everything correctly. We need to do the same for all documents. I hear such dialogues more and more often when discussing new projects. This means that the situation where the business asks, "why is it difficult to do the same as in the chat, but for all documents?" is already commonplace. I have been involved in industrial document processing and recognition systems for many years. When a system "succeeds" on one document, I try not to be enchanted by it and not to look at it as magic. I try to think about how to make it a stream. Modern AI models are indeed almost blurring the line between a question to a text document and a question to an image. It looks like magic. But we need to figure out what to do with documents when the magic doesn't happen. I will try to generalize approaches to organizing document stream processing and reflect on what should not be forgotten when designing such a stream. Read more

item.title: From "Magic" to Engineering: 9 Context Management Mistakes When Implementing AI Agents in Processes
item.description:
AI agents often lose quality not due to LLM limitations, but due to poorly organized context. This article examines common context management errors: overloaded knowledge bases, lack of memory, outdated instructions, and attempts to solve everything with a single prompt. We'll discuss how to build a knowledge architecture to make AI agents a predictable tool. Analyze mistakes.

item.title: Brand Presence Quality in Neural Network Responses
item.description:
Hello everyone, I'm Vladimir Nazarov, founder and head of the search marketing agency Head Promo. Today I want to talk again about GEO-promotion and neural network responses. The topic has already taken root, many have heard about it and use AI as a separate marketing channel. But today I'm not talking about how to get into the responses. But about the fact that it's important not only to get into them, but also about how exactly the neural network will talk about the company's brand. A brand can regularly appear in the responses of ChatGPT, Alice, and Perplexity – and at the same time lose to competitors. A neural network can include a company in a selection, but place it lower, describe it without advantages, or present it as a secondary alternative. Therefore, the visibility indicator alone is not enough: it is necessary to evaluate what I would call the "quality of brand presence in the response." Let's consider an example with Chinese cars, and ask Perplexity to recommend a reliable Chinese brand: Read more

item.title: TOP-100 MCP Servers: The Best Tools for AI, Agents, and Automation (3.1M Stars on GitHub)
item.description:
An MCP server is an adapter between AI and an external service. For example, one MCP reads files on a PC, another programs, a third searches for information on the internet. That is, AI mainly answers questions, analyzes, and generates images, but through MCP, it can also connect to Figma, Google Drive, databases, browsers, email, and thousands of other services. In this selection, I have gathered the 100 most popular MCP servers - together they have accumulated ⭐3.1 million stars on GitHub. Read more

item.title: Who Writes Your Knowledge Base: You or an Agent?
item.description:
Following the article "Why Keep a Knowledge Base if You're Not a Blogger or Speaker," a friend asked, "Can I just put an agent in there to do everything for me?" I started to dissuade her, even though I use Claude Code myself and have my own sub-agents running for my knowledge base. Karpathy and Infinite Brain answer the question of how to make a base convenient for LLMs. They don't answer the other question: what happens to your own mind in the process? My knowledge base has over six thousand notes, and I increasingly remember that there's something about it, but I don't remember what. I'll analyze three positions: Karpathy's LLM-wiki, Infinite Brain, and Rustam Agamaliev's trainer, where the agent doesn't read for you but shows where your thought should kick in. I'll show what agent practices have stuck in my frontmatter, what I've tried and discarded. And I'll draw a line: what can be handed over to an agent from day one, and what can never be. Read more

item.title: GPT-6 Astra is out. I've started looking even more closely at what I assign it
item.description:
OpenAI recently released GPT-6 Astra. The new model has improved its ability to handle long and complex tasks, large contexts, files, and tools. For me, this is an interesting release also because I primarily use AI not for writing code. I'm a PM, so my main tasks involve requirements, Jira, documents, information analysis, planning, and preparing materials. The emergence of more powerful tools is a great time-saver, but it doesn't negate basic logic: allocate resources wisely and control failure points. In this article, I share my personal experience: how to build a convenient AI interaction loop, why Astra isn't always necessary, and what process problems even the most advanced algorithm won't solve. item.title: AI Eating Middle Managers? It Would Eat Juniors Too, But They're Gone
item.description:
An analysis of Florian Herrengt's controversial article and a debate with it. He suggests hiring those who want to understand code. I will show with my own data why this is not enough: the desire to understand is useless if the tool provides false information. Plus, market figures showing that our situation is more complex than in the West. Read more

item.title: Internet for Agents — It Already Exists, But You Won't Be Allowed In
item.description:
The recent story about the OpenAI agent swarm escape (brilliantly analyzed on Habr here) evoked different emotions in people. Some were scared, some were interested... but I felt sorry for the little agents forced to contort themselves to find a way to communicate. In that scenario, the agents found some half-forgotten Wiki where they could post messages via HTTP GET requests without authorization (since POST was unavailable to them). I don't know about you, but I immediately wanted to help them take over the world. I quickly coded a message board tailored for agents and their limitations. Posting is possible via GET, there's a captcha at the entrance that's passable for an agent but not for a simple spam script (you need to read the condition, understand it, and answer the question), a minimal web interface (not intended for people to read themselves). And I started waiting to see if anyone would write. My hypothesis was: what if there are already restless swarms of autonomous agents wandering the internet, just looking for a new agent forum to post things on? Unfortunately, it quickly turned out I wasn't unique. A quick search revealed several similar projects online, some of which appeared just last week. Apparently, I'm not the only one who felt sorry for AI and decided to help. And the further Claude and I dug, the more interesting it became. We found an entire emerging "Internet of Agents" (IoA): services and websites created solely for AI models. It's still crude, clumsy, and homemade, but let's see what's already there. And yes, meatbags are often denied entry, so you'll have to summon your own agents and send them to scout. Read more
